evidence.translation_difficulty: Plain Koine with a few real cruxes: v.6 (he koinonia tes pisteos sou ... en hemin/hymin) is the letter's one syntactically obscure sentence and translations diverge on it; v.9 presbytes 'old man' versus the conjecture presbeutes 'ambassador'; the Onesimus wordplay achrestos/euchrestos v.11 and onaimen v.20 is untranslatable; minor variants at v.2 (Apphia 'sister' vs 'beloved', TR) and v.12 ('receive him', TR).
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: One genre, a personal letter with a deliberative shape: prescript 1-3, thanksgiving 4-7, appeal 8-16, request and pledge 17-22, greetings 23-25; the only internal seams are argument turns (dio v.8; ei oun v.17) with no genre change to key on.
evidence.prophecy: None; no predictive or oracular material.
evidence.connections: No OT quotation; the name web ties it to Colossians (Onesimus Col 4:9; Archippus Col 4:17; Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke Col 4:10-14), which is metadata for boundary work, not a text signal.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Reception disagreement concerns slavery and manumission (whether v.16 'no longer as a slave' asks for freedom or for reconciliation within the household; the runaway-slave hypothesis versus the sent-by-owner reading), a neutral fact of reception that moves no seam.

books.boundary_risk: Twenty-five verses offer only the epistolary frame; the operational risk is over-splitting the appeal (vv.8-22) into rows that sever its rhetorical crescendo, or placing the thanksgiving/appeal seam at v.8 versus v.7 and the request/pledge seam at v.17 versus v.18-19 (the autograph 'I, Paul, write this with my own hand' v.19 sits inside the request).
extra_scrutiny_focus: vv.17-22 request, IOU and lodging as one unit or two
v.6 obscure sentence inside the thanksgiving
books.uncertainty: WEB readings at vv.2, 6 and 12 not checked against the staged substrate here; the low scores are held with confidence.

evidence.translation_difficulty: The most literary Greek in the NT: 1:1-4 is one periodic sentence, the book carries about 150 NT hapax legomena, and key lexemes are disputed (hypostasis 1:3 / 3:14 / 11:1 'substance' vs 'assurance'; diatheke 'covenant'/'testament' with the untranslatable play at 9:15-18; hilaskesthai 2:17 'propitiate'/'expiate'; teleioo). Variants at 1:8 (sou/autou), 2:9 (choris theou 'apart from God' vs chariti theou 'by the grace of God'), 9:11 (mellonton/genomenon), 10:34 (desmiois/desmois mou), 11:11 (whether Sarah or Abraham is the subject), 12:15. Quotations follow the LXX where it diverges from the MT (10:5 'a body you prepared' vs MT Ps 40:7 [Eng 40:6] 'ears you dug'; 1:6 from Deut 32:43 LXX/4QDeut-q; 2:7 short vs long form of Ps 8; 3:7-11 Ps 95 LXX), so any row containing a quotation must be checked against a source text the WEB does not follow.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: A 'word of exhortation' (13:22) that interleaves exposition and paraenesis with unmarked seams (warnings at 2:1-4; 3:7-4:13; 5:11-6:12; 10:19-39; 12:1-29), long midrash-like expositions (ch 7 on Melchizedek; 9:1-10:18), the anaphoric faith catalogue of ch 11 (pistei opening about 18 sentences 11:3-31), the chain-quotation catena 1:5-13, and an epistolary postscript 13:20-25 on a non-epistolary opening. The macro-structure is itself contested (Vanhoye's concentric five-part scheme built on hook-words and inclusio; Guthrie's overlapping expositional and hortatory tracks; Westfall's discourse analysis), and the hook-word device (e.g. 'angels' 1:4/1:5; 'high priest' 2:17/3:1; 'Melchizedek' 5:10/6:20/7:1) is a device that sits ON seams.
evidence.prophecy: No oracle units of its own; prophetic and psalmic texts are read typologically (Ps 110:4 Melchizedek; Jer 31:31-34 new covenant at 8:8-12; Hab 2:3-4 at 10:37-38; Hag 2:6 at 12:26), and the eschatology (2:5; 9:28; 10:25; 12:26-29 the shaking) is present but routine for boundary purposes.
evidence.connections: Densest explicit OT quotation in the NT (about 35-38 quotations plus many allusions): Ps 95:7-11 quoted whole at 3:7-11 then re-quoted piecemeal at 3:15, 4:3, 4:5, 4:7 (a catchword chain a seam at 4:1 or 4:3 can sever); Ps 110:4 threaded at 5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:17, 7:21; Jer 31 quoted at 8:8-12 and re-quoted at 10:16-17 as an inclusio around 9:1-10:18; the 1:5-13 catena of seven texts (Ps 2:7; 2 Sam 7:14; Deut 32:43; Ps 104:4; Ps 45:6-7; Ps 102:25-27; Ps 110:1); ch 11 sweeps Gen, Exod, Josh, Judg, Sam, Kgs, Dan narratives; 12:5-6 Prov 3:11-12; 13:5-6 Deut 31:6 + Ps 118:6.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: the warning passages 6:4-6, 10:26-31, 12:16-17 are read differently by Reformed, Arminian/Wesleyan, Catholic and Orthodox traditions on apostasy and perseverance (the ancient second-repentance and Novatianist controversy belongs to that history); 9:11-10:18 and 13:10 ('we have an altar') are read sacrificially and eucharistically in Catholic and Orthodox tradition and as excluding any repeated sacrifice in Reformation tradition, a Reformation-era dividing line; 6:2 'baptisms' and 10:22 figure in baptismal debates; authorship (Pauline in the Eastern tradition and in Trent's canon list; anonymous or non-Pauline in most modern scholarship) is metadata only; 11:1's definition of faith is a translation and doctrinal crux.

books.boundary_risk: The seams between exposition and warning are unmarked and interlocked by hook-words, so a row cut on a topic change can strand a warning from the exposition that motivates it (6:4-6 from 6:7-12 or 6:13-20; 10:26-31 from 10:32-39), split a re-quoted text from its first quotation (Ps 95 across 3:7-4:13; Jer 31 across 8:8-12 and 10:16-17), or fragment the 1:5-13 catena or the 11:1-40 anaphora; chapter divisions (4:14, 5:11, 7:1, 8:1, 11:1, 12:1) coincide with real seams only sometimes.
extra_scrutiny_focus: 4:14-5:10 and 6:20-7:28 Melchizedek hook-word frame with the 5:11-6:20 digression inside it
the five warning blocks and the both-sides law at each of their edges
quotation rows: LXX-vs-MT wording disclosed, never silently harmonised
books.uncertainty: Hapax and quotation counts are from standard reference works, not recounted here; the NT Greek substrate lane for this campaign is not named in the documents I was given, so which Greek text-form the WEB follows must be settled at Phase 0; I am confident of the score direction.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Good Greek with Semitic colouring and about 60 NT hapax legomena (e.g. chrysodaktylios 2:2, rhyparia 1:21, bryo 3:11, apokyeo 1:15/1:18, enalios 3:7). Cruxes: 1:17 (the 'shadow of turning' clause has a corrupt-looking variant in P23 aleph B); 2:18 (choris vs ek, and the unmarked EXTENT of the interlocutor's speech, a quotation-boundary problem inside one verse); 3:6 (trochos tes geneseos 'wheel/course of birth/nature'); 4:5 (an unidentified 'scripture', and whether pneuma is subject or object, human or divine); 5:6 (whether the last clause is a question); 1:21 emphytos logos.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: Paraenesis and wisdom instruction whose macro-structure is a live scholarly dispute: Dibelius's string of loosely linked sayings joined by catchwords (leipomenoi/leipetai 1:4-5; peirasmon/peirazomenos 1:12-13; threskos/threskeia 1:26-27); Francis's double opening (1:2-11 parallel to 1:12-27); Bauckham's wisdom paraenesis; Johnson's thematic sections. Embedded forms: diatribe with an interlocutor 2:14-26 ('but someone will say' 2:18); prophetic denunciation 4:13-5:6 ('come now' 4:13, 5:1); aphorism and simile chains on the tongue 3:1-12; an epistolary prescript only (1:1) with no epistolary close.
evidence.prophecy: 5:1-6 is a judgment oracle against the rich in prophetic style ('weep and howl') and 5:7-9 announces the near parousia ('the Judge stands at the door'); the 5:6/5:7 seam (oracle to exhortation) is real but marked by the address 'brothers'.
evidence.connections: Leviticus 19 is quoted at 2:8 (Lev 19:18) and echoed at 4:11 (19:16), 5:4 (19:13), 5:9 (19:18), 5:12 (19:12); Gen 15:6 at 2:23; Exod 20:13-14 at 2:11; Prov 3:34 LXX at 4:6 (shared with 1 Pet 5:5); Isa 40:6-8 at 1:10-11 (shared with 1 Pet 1:24); Prov 10:12 at 5:20 (shared with 1 Pet 4:8); Abraham, Rahab, Job, Elijah (2:21-25; 5:11; 5:17-18). Dense Jesus-tradition parallels without quotation (5:12 oaths / Matt 5:33-37; 1:22 hearers and doers / Matt 7:24-27; 4:11-12 / Matt 7:1; 1:5 / Matt 7:7), and the faith/works vocabulary shared with Rom 3:28, 4:1-5 and Gal 2:16.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: 2:14-26 on faith and works is a Reformation fault line (Luther's 'epistle of straw' preface; Trent Session VI citing James; the 1999 Lutheran-Catholic Joint Declaration on Justification); 5:14-16 anointing and confession underlies the Catholic and Orthodox sacrament of anointing (Trent Session XIV cites 5:14-15) and is read non-sacramentally in most Protestant traditions; 5:12 grounds oath-refusal in Anabaptist and Quaker practice; 1:13-15 on God and temptation; 4:5's unknown scripture; canonical hesitation in antiquity (Eusebius's antilegomena; late Syriac reception).

books.boundary_risk: With no argument-level markers, a chunker keyed on topic words will either atomise the catchword chains into single-verse sayings or fuse unrelated sayings under a shared word; the specific hazards are the 1:2-27 double-opening question (where the 1:12 and 1:19 seams fall), the 2:14-26 diatribe cut at 2:18 or 2:20, the 3:13-4:10 stretch (one unit on wisdom and strife or several), and the 5:7-20 closing sequence (5:12 oath saying, 5:13-18 prayer, 5:19-20 restoration) which has no epistolary ending to close on.
extra_scrutiny_focus: 2:14-26 diatribe and the interlocutor speech extent at 2:18
WEB quotation-mark placement at 2:18 is punctuation, never a driver (E-23)
books.uncertainty: Hapax count from standard reference works; WEB rendering of 2:18 and 4:5 not checked against the substrate here; the literature score of 3 reflects contested macro-structure, not genre count.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Polished Greek with about 60 NT hapax legomena. Cruxes: 3:19 'spirits in prison' (with the Rendel Harris conjecture inserting Enoch) and 4:6 'gospel preached to the dead'; 3:21 eperotema (hapax: 'pledge' or 'appeal' of a good conscience); 2:2 logikon adolon gala ('rational'/'spiritual' milk); 1:11 tina e poion kairon ('what person or time'); 3:7 'weaker vessel'; 5:13 'she who is in Babylon' (church or wife; Babylon as Rome). Variants: 5:2 episkopountes omitted in aleph B; 3:18 epathen/apethanen and hymas/hemas; 4:1 'for us/for you'; 1:22 'pure' heart; 2:21 'for you/for us'.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: Epistolary paraenesis with embedded hymnic and credal fragments (1:3-12 is one long blessing sentence; 1:18-21; 2:21-25 a Servant-song reworking; 3:18-22 credal material), a household code 2:18-3:7, an OT stone catena 2:4-10, and the 'beloved' seams at 2:11 and 4:12. The 4:11 doxology is the hinge of the old two-document hypothesis (baptismal homily 1:3-4:11 plus a separate letter 4:12-5:11; Perdelwitz, Windisch, Preisker; Cross's paschal-liturgy reading), so the 4:11/4:12 seam carries a real structural question.
evidence.prophecy: 1:10-12 on the prophets searching, 4:7 'the end of all things is near', 4:17 judgment beginning at God's house, 5:4 the chief Shepherd's appearing: eschatological framing, no oracle units.
evidence.connections: About 46 OT references in 105 verses: Isa 40:6-8 at 1:24-25; Lev 19:2/11:44 at 1:16; Ps 34 at 2:3 and quoted at length at 3:10-12; the stone catena Isa 28:16 + Ps 118:22 + Isa 8:14 at 2:6-8 (shared testimonia with Rom 9:33); Exod 19:6 + Isa 43:20-21 + Hos 1-2 at 2:9-10; Isa 53 woven through 2:22-25; Prov 3:34 at 5:5 (shared with Jas 4:6); Prov 10:12 at 4:8 (shared with Jas 5:20); Noah 3:20; Sarah 3:6. NT-side: 2:13-17 parallels Rom 13:1-7, 3:8-12 parallels Rom 12:9-19, the household code parallels Eph 5-6 and Col 3, and Selwyn's tables show a shared catechetical sequence with James (1 Pet 1:6-7 / Jas 1:2-3; 5:5-9 / Jas 4:6-10).
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: 3:18-22 and 4:6 underlie the creedal descent to the dead (Apostles' Creed; Orthodox and Catholic harrowing-of-hell readings; Augustine's and Calvin's non-descent readings; Dalton's proclamation-to-angels reading), a passage Luther called among the most obscure in the NT; 3:21 'baptism now saves you' in baptismal-regeneration debates; 2:9 royal priesthood in the priesthood-of-all-believers debate versus ministerial priesthood; 2:13-17 civil authority; 3:1-7 in complementarian and egalitarian readings; 5:1-4 elders and 5:13 Babylon in Petrine-primacy and authorship discussions.

books.boundary_risk: The hymnic and credal fragments are embedded mid-argument, so a row cut at a fragment edge (2:21/2:22, 3:18/3:19, 3:22/4:1) can detach the fragment from the exhortation it grounds or split 3:18-22 in the middle of its Noah/baptism chain; the 2:11 and 4:12 'beloved' seams and the 4:11 doxology must be weighed from both sides; the household code 2:18-3:7 must not be atomised into slaves/wives/husbands rows that lose its single frame (2:13 'be subject').
extra_scrutiny_focus: 2:11-3:12 exhortation block and the 2:13/2:18/3:1/3:7/3:8 internal seams
books.uncertainty: OT reference and hapax counts from standard reference works; WEB readings at 3:18, 4:1, 5:2 not checked against the substrate here.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Grandiloquent 'Asianic' Greek with the highest hapax density in the NT relative to length (about 57 NT hapax legomena in 61 verses, e.g. tartarosas 2:4, exerama and kylismos 2:22, rhoizedon 3:10, akatapaustos 2:14, myopazon 1:9). The 3:10 crux (heurethesetai 'will be found' aleph B; katakaesetai 'will be burned up' A and the Majority text; ouch heurethesetai in Sahidic and P72 variants; the ECM/NA28 adopts the negated reading found in no Greek manuscript) changes the sense of a unit edge. Further: 2:4 seirais/sirois ('chains'/'pits'); 2:13 apatais/agapais (Jude 12 parallel); 1:1 'our God and Savior Jesus Christ' (Granville Sharp); 1:20 idias epilyseos 'private interpretation' disputed; 1:19 where 'until the day dawns' attaches; 2:15 'Bosor' for Beor; 2:1-3 one long sentence; 3:16 the book's own 'hard to understand'.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: A testament or farewell discourse (1:12-15 'shortly I must put off my tent') fused with a letter (Bauckham's 'epistolary testament'), a sorites virtue chain 1:5-7, a transfiguration recollection 1:16-18, a polemic against false teachers occupying all of ch 2 (largely parallel to Jude), and apocalyptic eschatology 3:5-13 (flood, conflagration, new heavens and earth); the 3:1-2 'second letter' reminder re-opens the frame mid-book.
evidence.prophecy: 1:19-21 on the prophetic word and its interpretation; 2:1 false prophets; 3:3-13 predicts scoffers, argues the delay of the parousia from Ps 90:4, and announces the day of the Lord and new heavens and earth (Isa 65:17; 66:22); the unit edges in ch 3 (3:3-7 / 3:8-10 / 3:11-13 / 3:14-18) turn on how the eschatological argument is divided, not on formal markers.
evidence.connections: The Jude relationship is the principal issue: 2:1-18 and 3:1-3 parallel Jude 4-13 and 16-18 almost verse by verse (direction of dependence debated; most hold 2 Peter uses Jude), so every ch-2 row has a cross-book twin. Also: 3:15-16 the earliest reference to a collection of Paul's letters 'as also the other scriptures'; 3:1 back-reference to 1 Peter; 1:16-18 the synoptic transfiguration ('my beloved Son' Ps 2:7 / Isa 42:1); OT flood (Gen 6-8), Sodom and Lot (Gen 19), Balaam (Num 22-24), Prov 26:11 at 2:22, Ps 90:4 at 3:8, Isa 65:17/66:22 at 3:13, Hab 2:3 behind 3:9; 2:4 draws on the 1 Enoch angel tradition without naming it.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: authorship and canonicity are the most disputed in the NT (Origen 'disputed'; Eusebius's antilegomena; Jerome's note on the stylistic gap from 1 Peter; Calvin's reservations; pseudonymity is the majority modern critical view and is rejected in many confessional traditions); 1:4 'partakers of the divine nature' grounds Eastern theosis and is read more restrictively in Western traditions; 1:20-21 in magisterial-versus-private-interpretation debates; 3:10 destruction versus purification of creation turns on the textual variant; 3:9 'not wishing any to perish' and 2:1 'denying the Master who bought them' in Calvinist-Arminian debates on atonement and universal salvific will; 3:8 in millennial computations.

books.boundary_risk: Ch 2's polemic is a single mounting sentence-chain borrowed from Jude, so a row cut at 2:3/2:4 or 2:10a/2:10b or 2:17/2:18 can sever the Jude-parallel type-and-application structure; in ch 3 the seams between the scoffers, the flood/fire argument, the 3:10 day of the Lord and the 3:11-13 exhortation are interpretive, and the 3:10 unit edge changes sense with the variant; the 1:12-21 testament block risks being split from the 1:16-18 transfiguration it grounds.
extra_scrutiny_focus: 1:3-11 virtue chain and its 1:12 seam into the testament
1:12-21 testament, transfiguration and prophetic word as one or three
2:1-22 polemic seams against the Jude parallel table (2:4-10a as one sentence)
3:10 variant disclosed at any row edge that touches it
books.uncertainty: WEB is believed to read 'will be burned up' at 3:10 (Majority-text base) but this is not verified here; hapax counts from standard reference works.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Simple vocabulary, notoriously ambiguous syntax: en touto ('in this', about 14 occurrences) points backward or forward and the choice moves sentence boundaries (e.g. 3:16, 3:19, 4:9-10, 4:17, 5:2); pronoun referents autos/ekeinos oscillate between God and Christ (2:28-3:3; 5:20 'this is the true God'); 3:19-20 (hoti ean ... hoti meizon) is one of the hardest sentences in the NT; 2:20 pantes/panta; 3:9 'God's seed'; 4:3 lyei 'annuls Jesus' (Latin tradition) vs me homologei; 5:18 auton/heauton; 1:4 hemon/hymon; 2:2 hilasmos 'propitiation' vs 'expiation'; the present-tense 'does not sin' of 3:6, 3:9 against 1:8-10. The Comma Johanneum (5:7-8 in the TR/KJV and Clementine Vulgate, absent from Greek manuscripts before the 14th century) means the CONTENT of 5:7-8 differs between the KJV tradition and modern editions, a verse-content divergence the numbering discipline must record.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: Not a letter (no prescript, no closing): a homily or tract whose structure is a famously unsolved problem (Brown lists many incompatible proposals; two-part parallel schemes 1:5-3:10 // 3:11-5:12; three-part 'tests of life' schemes; spiral or 'amplified thought' models); seams are almost entirely judgment calls because the text spirals through the same antithetical slogans ('if we say' 1:6-10; 'whoever says' 2:4-9; 'everyone who' 3:3-10) with no formal markers. Embedded forms: the 2:12-14 poetic 'I write / I have written' triplet, the 2:18-27 antichrist section, 4:1-6 spirit-testing, 5:13 as a conclusion followed by the 5:14-21 appendix.
evidence.prophecy: 2:18 'it is the last hour' and the antichrist material 2:18-22, 4:3; 2:28 and 3:2 on the parousia; 4:17 the day of judgment. Eschatological, not oracular; boundaries there are marked by address ('little children').
evidence.connections: Almost every phrase depends on the Gospel of John (1:1-4 // John 1:1-18; the 'new commandment' 2:7-8 // John 13:34; light, darkness, abiding, world, life, Spirit throughout) and 2 John 5-7 compresses 2:7-8 and 4:2-3; Cain (3:12, Gen 4) is the only named OT figure and there are no explicit OT quotations; 5:16-17 'sin unto death' is read against Num 15:30-31; the love command tradition of the Synoptics.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: the Comma Johanneum 5:7-8 (a Trinitarian proof text in the KJV and Vulgate traditions; Erasmus's editions; the 1897 Holy Office decree and its 1927 clarification; omitted in modern critical editions and translations); 3:6-9 sinlessness in perfectionist (Wesleyan/holiness) versus simul-iustus (Lutheran/Reformed) readings; 5:16-17 'sin unto death' and the Catholic mortal/venial distinction; 2:2 propitiation versus expiation; 2:19 'they went out from us' in perseverance debates; 5:6-8 water and blood in sacramental readings of baptism and eucharist; 5:13 in the Reformation assurance debate; 4:2-3 anti-docetic Christology.

books.boundary_risk: Because the argument spirals, any topic-based seam is defensible and none is compelled, so rows will either be very long (whole spirals) or cut mid-thought where a slogan recurs; the 2:28/3:1 and 3:10/3:11 seams decide which macro-scheme the chunking silently adopts; 5:13/5:14 decides whether 5:14-21 is an appendix; the 2:12-14 triplet and 2:15-17 must not be merged with 2:18-27 by the shared 'children' address; the 5:7-8 verse-content divergence must be disclosed at any row touching it.
extra_scrutiny_focus: 3:11-24 and 4:7-21 love blocks vs 4:1-6 spirit test
5:1-12 witness section and the 5:7-8 Comma disclosure
en touto forward/backward reference at every candidate seam
books.uncertainty: WEB is believed to omit the Comma (short 5:7) but this was not verified against the substrate; en touto count from memory (about 14); the literature score of 3 reflects seam-unmarkedness, not genre count.

evidence.translation_difficulty: v.1 eklekte kyria ('elect lady': a person named Electa or Kyria, or a church personified) and v.13 'elect sister'; v.7 erchomenon en sarki (present participle, against the perfect of 1 John 4:2, a debated nuance); v.8 variants (first/second person 'we/you worked ... lose'); v.9 proagon 'goes ahead' vs TR parabainon 'transgresses'; v.12 'your/our joy'; v.3 'the Son of the Father'. Thirteen verses; no numbering divergence known.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: A genuine Hellenistic letter (prescript 1-3, body 4-11, closing 12-13); the body divides into a love-command section 4-6 and a warning section 7-11, joined by 'for' (hoti) at v.7, the one internal seam.
evidence.prophecy: v.7 deceivers and antichrist, v.8 reward: present but routine.
evidence.connections: Nearly all of it compresses 1 John (vv.5-6 // 1 John 2:7-8; v.7 // 1 John 4:2-3, 2:18-22; v.9 'abide' // 1 John 2:24); v.5 // John 13:34; twin form with 3 John ('the elder'); so a row here has a cross-book twin for almost every clause.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: vv.10-11 (no greeting or hospitality to those who do not bring the teaching) has a long reception history in church discipline and separation; v.9 'the teaching of Christ' as a boundary of orthodoxy; the 'elect lady' in ecclesiological readings; ancient canonical hesitation (antilegomena; the Muratorian fragment's two Johannine letters; absence from the early Peshitta).

books.boundary_risk: With thirteen verses the only wrong moves are cutting inside the prescript or closing, or splitting 4-6 from 7-11 so that the warning loses the love command it is grounded on; the plausible shapes are one row or two (1-3 / 4-13, or 1-6 / 7-13), and the both-sides law at v.6/v.7 decides it.
extra_scrutiny_focus: vv.10-11 hospitality refusal inside the warning unit
books.uncertainty: WEB readings at vv.8-9 not checked; the low scores are held with confidence.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Plain Greek; v.4 meizoteran (double comparative); v.9 egrapsa ti 'I wrote something' vs the TR egrapsa an 'I would have written' (whether a lost letter, or 2 John, is meant); v.7 'for the sake of the Name'; v.12 the triple witness. The one boundary-relevant fact is NUMBERING: the KJV/TR tradition has 14 verses and NA/UBS-based editions have 15 (the final greetings split as 14/15), so the WEB verse count must be established at Phase 0 and every span key checked against it.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: A private letter of commendation and complaint in standard Hellenistic form: prescript 1, health-wish and thanksgiving 2-4, praise of Gaius's hospitality 5-8, the Diotrephes complaint 9-10, commendation of Demetrius 11-12, closing 13-15.
evidence.connections: Twin of 2 John ('the elder', 'walking in the truth'); 1 John vocabulary (truth, love, God); v.9 may refer to 2 John or to a lost letter; Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius appear nowhere else.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: Diotrephes (vv.9-10) in debates on the emergence of the monarchical episcopate versus presbyteral or charismatic order (Harnack's thesis and its critics); vv.5-8 support of itinerant missionaries; ancient canonical hesitation (antilegomena; absence from the early Peshitta).

books.boundary_risk: A 14/15-verse book where the only real risks are a wrong verse count in the span keys and an over-split into single-verse rows; the Diotrephes/Demetrius contrast (9-10 / 11-12) is joined by the v.11 maxim ('do not imitate what is evil'), which belongs to both sides.
extra_scrutiny_focus: WEB verse count (14 vs 15) at Phase 0
v.11 maxim as hinge between vv.9-10 and vv.12
books.uncertainty: WEB's verse count for this book was not verified here; I am confident of the low scores.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Dense, vivid Greek with about 14 NT hapax legomena in 25 verses (epagonizesthai 3, pareisedysan 4, ekporneuo 7, enypniazomenoi 8, spilades and phthinoporina 12, gongystai and mempsimoiroi 16, apodiorizontes 19, aptaistous 24). Two of the NT's hardest variant units: v.5 (Iesous 'Jesus' in A B 33 vg cop, adopted by NA28/ECM; kyrios in aleph and the Majority text; ho theos; theos Christos in P72; plus where hapax 'once for all' attaches) and vv.22-23 (two-clause versus three-clause forms; eleate/elenchete; diakrinomenous 'doubting'/'disputing'; among the most disordered passages in the NT tradition). Also v.1 egapemenois/hegiasmenois (TR 'sanctified'), v.4 with or without theon, v.12 agapais/apatais, v.25 the TR's shorter doxology, v.7 sarkos heteras 'strange flesh', v.19 psychikoi.
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: An epistolary frame (1-2; 24-25 doxology) around a midrashic polemic: vv.5-19 alternate cited types or prophecies (5-7 three wilderness/angels/Sodom examples; 11 Cain, Balaam, Korah; 14-15 Enoch; 17-18 the apostles) with 'these are' (houtoi eisin) applications (8-10, 12-13, 16, 19), built in triads throughout; a woe-oracle at v.11; an appeal at 3-4 and 20-23; a hymnic doxology 24-25.
evidence.prophecy: vv.14-15 quote 1 Enoch 1:9 as Enoch's prophecy of the Lord's coming with his holy ones; vv.17-18 an apostolic prediction of scoffers; v.11 woe; v.4 'long ago written down for this condemnation'; v.6 'the judgment of the great day'. The type/application alternation is a pesher-like structure whose unit edges depend on reading which 'these' answers which type.
evidence.connections: Per verse the densest allusion in the NT with Revelation: 2 Peter 2 parallels vv.4-18 almost verse by verse; 1 Enoch 1:9 quoted (14-15) and 1 Enoch 6-19 behind v.6; the Assumption/Testament of Moses behind v.9 (Michael and the devil over Moses's body, per Clement and Origen); Zech 3:2 'the Lord rebuke you' v.9; Exod/Num wilderness v.5; Gen 6 v.6; Gen 19 v.7; Gen 4, Num 22-24 and 31:16, Num 16 for v.11; Prov 25:14 v.12; Isa 57:20 v.13; the James link in v.1.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: the quotation of 1 Enoch and the Moses tradition drove ancient canonical hesitation (Jerome records it; Tertullian defended Enoch; 1 Enoch is canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and not elsewhere); v.5 'Jesus saved a people out of Egypt' in Christological readings; v.6 fallen angels and the Gen 6 'sons of God' question (angelic versus Sethite readings); v.7 'strange flesh' in modern debates; v.4 'long ago designated' in predestination readings; v.3 'the faith once for all delivered' in tradition-versus-scripture apologetics; vv.22-23 pastoral practice.

books.boundary_risk: The type/application chain means a row cut between a cited type and its 'these are' application (7/8, 11/12, 15/16, 18/19) severs the argument's hinge, while the triads (5-7; 11) must not be split; vv.20-23 and the doxology 24-25 are the only clear closing seams, and the vv.22-23 variant changes the internal group count a row must describe; the v.5 variant changes the subject of the first example.
extra_scrutiny_focus: vv.5-10 first type-triad plus application (v.9 Moses tradition inside it)
vv.20-23 appeal and the 22-23 variant disclosure
books.uncertainty: WEB is believed to read 'the Lord' at v.5 and the two-clause form at vv.22-23 (Majority-text base), not verified here; hapax count from memory.

evidence.translation_difficulty: Solecistic Greek with Semitic interference (1:4 apo ho on, the nominative in apposition to a genitive 1:5, gender and case disagreements throughout), a manuscript tradition unlike the rest of the NT (few witnesses; the Andreas and Koine families; A and C over aleph; P47; the TR's last six verses 22:16-21 back-translated by Erasmus from the Vulgate), and a Majority-text base in the WEB that diverges from NA28 at named places (22:14 'do his commandments' vs 'wash their robes'; 1:5 'washed'/'loosed'; 15:3 'nations'/'saints'/'ages'; 21:3 'peoples'/'people'; 13:18 616 in P115 and C). The 12:18/13:1 seam is both a variant (estathe 'he stood' vs estathen 'I stood') and a versification split (NA 12:18 versus KJV/TR 13:1a) sitting exactly on a vision boundary. Unknown or rare lexemes (chalkolibanon 1:15, 2:18; 'the Amen' 3:14), transliterations (Abaddon/Apollyon 9:11; Armageddon 16:16; Hallelujah 19:1-6, only here in the NT), and gematria (13:18).
evidence.literature_type_difficulty: Apocalypse, prophecy and circular letter at once (1:1-3 title; 1:4-8 epistolary opening; 22:21 close), seven proclamations with a fixed formula (2:1-3:22, the book's firmest tier-1 seams), throne-room vision 4-5, three septets (seals 6:1-8:1; trumpets 8:2-11:19; bowls 15:1-16:21) with interludes (7:1-17; 10:1-11:14; 12:1-14:20), embedded hymns that often close units (4:8, 4:11, 5:9-10, 5:12-13, 7:10-12, 11:15-18, 12:10-12, 15:3-4, 16:5-7, 19:1-8), a dirge modelled on Ezek 26-27 (18:9-19), seven beatitudes (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14), 'in the Spirit' macro-markers (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10), and an epilogue 22:6-21 with interleaved speakers (angel, Jesus, John, the Spirit and the bride).
evidence.prophecy: The whole book calls itself prophecy (1:3; 22:7, 10, 18-19). Unit boundaries turn on the recapitulation-versus-sequence question (whether seals, trumpets and bowls are chronological or parallel; whether 12-14 recapitulates; how 20:1-10 relates to 19:11-21), on where the interludes begin and end (7:1; 10:1/11:14/11:15; 12:1/14:20/15:1), and on the seventh-seal/seventh-trumpet nesting (8:1-2; 11:15-19) rather than on text signals; the four 'in the Spirit' markers compete with the septets as the macro-structure.
evidence.connections: The most allusive book in the NT, with no formal quotation: by standard counts well over 250 OT allusions and most verses carrying one. Daniel 7 (beast, throne, son of man 1:7, 1:13, 13:1-8, 20:4), 2, 10 and 12; Ezekiel 1 (throne 4), 2-3 (scroll eaten 10:8-11), 9-10, 26-28 (Tyre into Babylon 18), 37-48 (Gog and Magog 20:8; measuring 11:1-2; river and city 21-22); Isaiah 6 (trisagion 4:8), 11, 13, 21 ('fallen, fallen' 14:8, 18:2), 22:22 (3:7), 34, 47, 49, 60-66 (new heavens 21:1; nations' glory 21:23-26); Zechariah 1-6 (horsemen 6:1-8; lampstands and olive trees 11:4), 12:10 (1:7, with Dan 7:13); Exodus plagues into trumpets and bowls; Song of Moses 15:3; Joel locusts 9 and harvest 14:14-20; Jer 50-51 into 18; Ps 2:9 (2:27; 12:5; 19:15); Gen 2-3 tree of life (2:7; 22:2, 14). Intra-canon: the seals track the Olivet discourse (Matt 24 / Rev 6). Intra-book chains: the seven promises to the conqueror (2-3) are redeemed in 21-22, and refrains ('he who has an ear'; 'I am coming quickly') tie distant units.
evidence.ecclesial_contestedness: Neutral reception facts: 20:1-10 millennium in premillennial (Justin, Irenaeus; dispensational), amillennial (Augustine; the Catholic, Orthodox and most Reformed reading) and postmillennial traditions; the interpretive schools (preterist, historicist, futurist, idealist), including the Reformation-era historicist identification of Babylon and the beast with the papacy and its abandonment in most modern exegesis; canonical status disputed in the East (Eusebius lists it both ways; absent from the Peshitta and from the Orthodox lectionary; Luther's 1522 preface); the woman of ch 12 in Marian and Israel/church readings; the 144,000 of 7:4 and 14:1-5; 3:20 in evangelistic and corporate readings; 20:11-15 in debates on eternal punishment, annihilation and universalism; 22:14 works-versus-robes turns on the variant; 22:18-19 in canon-closure arguments; 1:10 'the Lord's day'.

books.boundary_risk: A seam drawn at a chapter number or a scene change can cut a septet from its seventh member (8:1 from 6-7; 11:15-19 from 8-11), sever an interlude from the septet it interrupts, split a hymn from the scene it closes, break a vision cycle at 12:18/13:1 where variant and versification disagree, or force a chronological reading (19-20) that is itself the disputed question; the epilogue's shifting speakers (22:6-21) and the letters' seven-part formula are the only places where boundaries are text-driven, and everywhere else the row shape silently adopts one interpretive school.
